q: Who was the excavator of Lothal?
explanation: S.R. Rao excavated Lothal (discovered 1954, dug 1955-60). Daya Ram Sahni dug Harappa, A. Ghosh found Kalibangan and J.P. Joshi dug Surkotada.

notes.text: ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.79-83; old app notes row 7

q: Which of the following is not a Harappan site?
explanation: Sohgaura, on the Rapti near Gorakhpur, is a Mauryan-era copper-plate site and is not Harappan. Sutkagendor, Surkotada and Rakhigarhi are Harappan sites.

notes.text: - **Mohenjodaro** = "Mound of the Dead" (Sindhi; Lothal means the same in Gujarati); **Kalibangan** = "black bangles"; Dholavira local name **Kotada**.

q: Which was the first metal to be used by man?
explanation: Copper was the first metal used by man. Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, and iron came much later.

notes.text: - **Copper = the first metal used by man** (not iron, bronze, gold or silver); chalcolithic cultures began with it (APPSC G2 2011, RAS 2012).

q: The traces of the cultivation In Harappan Culture were found at:
explanation: Rice husks – the trace of rice cultivation – were found at Lothal and Rangpur; Kalibangan has a ploughed field, but Ropar gives no cultivation evidence, so Lothal and Rangpur is the pair.

q: Harappan people had close external contact with:
explanation: Mesopotamia was the Harappans' closest external contact: Harappan seals at Ur, Susa and Nippur, and Mesopotamian texts naming Meluhha. Bahrain (Dilmun) was only an intermediate station and Egypt shows no Harappan finds.

notes.text: - **Closest external contact = Mesopotamia** (not Egypt): Harappan seals at **Susa, Ur, Nippur**, Failaka, Bahrain; three Mesopotamian cylinder seals at Mohenjodaro; Dilmun weights followed the Harappan standard.

exam: APPSC Forest Range Officer Mains Paper-I General Studies & M
q: One of the distinctive features of Indus Valley Civilization is in the form of
options: Preservation of large amount of DNA
explanation: Seals are the most distinctive artefact of the IVC. Megaliths belong to later South India, no royal palaces have been found, and DNA preservation is not a defining feature.

notes.text: - With the script unread, **seals** are the **main source** of knowledge about the Harappan people (RAS 1996); broadly, the culture is known only from **archaeological excavations** (UPPSC 1993) – no inscriptions read, no religious books.
- **Uses:** facilitating **long-distance communication** and trade (APPSC G1 → **seals and sealings**), authentication, **ownership**, amulets – **not coins**.

q: Which of the following was mostly used to facilitate long distance communication by the inhabitants of Harappan Civilization?
explanation: Seals and sealings facilitated long-distance communication: an intact sealing on a package showed the goods were untouched and named the sender. Palm leaves and stone tablets were not used.

notes.text: - **Uses:** facilitating **long-distance communication** and trade (APPSC G1 → **seals and sealings**), authentication, **ownership**, amulets – **not coins**.

q: The measuring scale found at an Indus site is at
explanation: The ivory measuring scale was found at Lothal (a shell scale is also known from Mohenjodaro, but the classic answer is Lothal).

q: Which Indus Valley City a scale has been discovered?
explanation: An ivory scale was discovered at Lothal.

q: Which of the following birds was worshipped by the Harappa People?
explanation: NextGen lists the pigeon (dove) among the Harappans' sacred symbols, so pigeon is right; the peacock appears only as a pottery motif, and crow and eagle are not attested.

notes.text: - **Pigeon (dove):** listed by NextGen among sacred symbols – the bird "worshipped" by the Harappans (APPSC Group-II 2011); the peacock is only a pottery motif.

q: The late Harappan cultures are primarily Chalcolithic in which tools of stone and copper are used. 5. II. They do not show metal objects requiring complicated casting. III. The Chalcolithic people in the later Harappan phase lived in villages. IV. In the late Harappan phase at Bhagwanpura in Haryana, burnt bricks were not found.
explanation: I, II and III are correct: Late Harappan cultures were chalcolithic (stone and copper tools), lacked complex cast metal objects, and were village-based. IV is wrong: the Late Harappan people at Bhagwanpura lived in burnt-brick houses (some baked bricks occur there).

notes.text: - **APPSC Group-1 statements:** I chalcolithic ✓, II no complicated casting ✓, III villages ✓, IV no burnt bricks at Bhagwanpura ✗ → **I, II and III**.

- **Bhagwanpura (Kurukshetra, Haryana):** Late Harappan houses of **burnt brick** (so "no burnt bricks at Bhagwanpura" is **false**); Late Harappan pottery overlaps with **PGW**; a 13-roomed house (excavated by **J.P. Joshi**).

exam: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer (Mains) P
q: Avesta was written in ____ language.
explanation: The Avesta, the Zoroastrian scripture and oldest Iranian text, is in Avestan, an old Iranian language close to Rig Vedic Sanskrit.

notes.text: - **Avesta:** the **oldest Iranian** (Zoroastrian) text, in **Avestan, an old Iranian language**; closely similar to the Rig Veda → relates to **Iran** (UP Lower Sub 2004; APPSC FBO).

q: Which of the following inscriptions mentions the names of Vedic Gods Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatyas?
explanation: The Boghazkoi inscription (c. 1380 BCE, Asia Minor) records a Hittite–Mitanni treaty naming Indra, Mitra, Varuna and the Nasatyas. Mansehra and Shahbazgarhi are Ashokan rock edicts; Junagarh has Rudradaman's record.

notes.text: - **⚠ Trap:** Mansehra and Shahbazgarhi are Ashokan rock edicts; Junagarh is Rudradaman's – none names Vedic gods.

exam: APPSC 2018 Special Qualifying Test for Appointment by Promot
q: The administrative setup of early Aryans was in the nature of?
explanation: The early Aryans had a kinship-based tribal polity: the Rajan was a tribal chief, protector of the tribe and cattle, with no fixed territory or standing army.

notes.text: - **Tribal polity:** kinship-based **tribal chiefdom** (APPSC SQT 2018) – no formal bureaucracy, **no fixed territory**, no standing army.

q: This was the status of an Indian woman in the Vedic period
explanation: Women in the (Rig) Vedic age enjoyed a relatively good status – education, choice of husband, attendance at assemblies, no child marriage – within a patriarchal society, so 'somewhat superior' (compared with later periods). 'Very low' fits later periods, and 'sororate' is a marriage custom, not a status.

notes.text: - **Family:** **patriarchal, patrilineal, patrilocal**, joint (three generations) under the kulapa; **monogamy** usual.

q: In which of the following great texts is the Purusha Sukta found?
explanation: The Purusha Sukta is hymn X.90 of the Rigveda (10th Mandala, a late addition), describing the origin of the four varnas.

notes.text: - **Women seers (brahmavadinis):** **Lopamudra** (wife of **Agastya**, who Aryanised **South India**), **Ghosha**, **Apala**, **Vishvavara** – Rig Vedic (UPSC 1995).

q: The first reference to the fourfold caste system is found in:
explanation: The Purusha Sukta (Rigveda X.90) gives the first reference to the four-fold varna division; it is part of the Rigveda, but the specific answer is the Purusha Sukta.

notes.text: - **Women seers (brahmavadinis):** **Lopamudra** (wife of **Agastya**, who Aryanised **South India**), **Ghosha**, **Apala**, **Vishvavara** – Rig Vedic (UPSC 1995).

q: The sage who is said to have Aryanised South India was:
explanation: Sage Agastya is traditionally credited with spreading Vedic (Aryan) culture into South India; Apastamba was a Sutra author, Vasishtha and Vishvamitra northern Rigvedic priests.

notes.text: - **Agastya** = the sage said to have **Aryanised South India** (crossed the Vindhyas); not Vishvamitra, Vasishtha or Apastamba.

q: Hastinapura can be identified with which one of the following modern cities?
explanation:
Key / most books: Delhi. Strictly: Hastinapur lies in Meerut district (UP), ~96 km NE of Delhi; Delhi is Indraprastha (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastinapur).
Hastinapura, the Kuru capital, is the option associated with Delhi (Indraprastha) among those given; the site itself lies in Meerut district, UP.

q:
Consider the following types of pottery: 6.
I. Black and Red Ware
II. Black Slipped Ware
III. Painted Grey Ware
IV. Red Ware
V. Northern Black Polished Ware
Which of the above types of pottery were associated with the Later Vedic people?
options: I, II, III, IV and V 7
explanation:
APPSC key (G1 2024): II, III and IV only. R.S. Sharma and PMF list four Later Vedic wares including Black-and-Red Ware.
Later Vedic people knew four wares: Red ware, Black-slipped ware, Black-and-red ware and Painted Grey Ware, i.e. I, II, III and IV. Only NBPW (from c. 600 BCE, post-Vedic) is excluded. (official key: II, III and IV only)

notes.text: - Iron technology about **1000–800 BCE**; common at most **PGW sites** of the Doab; iron weapons (arrowheads, spearheads) common in western UP from about 800 BCE.

exam: APPSC 2023 Screening test (Online Mode) to the post of Deput
q: The pottery from 1000 B.C. to 600 B.C. found in the Gangetic plain is called the ________pottery.
explanation: Painted Grey Ware is the pottery of the Later Vedic period (1000-600 BC) in the Gangetic plain; the other names are not wares of this sequence.

notes.text: - **Jakhera** (UP): iron in the **Black and Red Ware phase, before 1200 BCE**; iron in Dharwar (Karnataka) c. 1000 BCE.

q: Describing social stratification using the order of Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra is called
explanation: Ordering society as Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra is the varna system; caste (jati) is the later, multiple birth groups.

notes.text: - Society stratified in the order **Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra** = the **Varna system** (varna came to rest on **birth**; spread of jatis is post-Vedic).

q: How many Ashrams are described in Vedas?
explanation: Four ashramas are described: Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha and Sannyasa.

notes.text: - **Four ashramas** are described; they are the custom that **emerged in the post-Vedic (Later Vedic) period** – the varnas go back to the Rigveda's Purusha Sukta and Indra-Surya-Rudra-Maruts are Rigvedic gods.

q: Marriage due to mutual love is called as?
explanation: Gandharva marriage rested on the mutual consent (love) of the two parties; Rakshasa was by capture and Asura by purchase.

q: The woman eminent in Vedic literature
explanation: Maitreyi, wife of Yajnavalkya, is the learned woman of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad; Shakuntala and Madalasa are epic/Puranic figures.

notes.text: - Learned women of Vedic literature: **Gargi, Maitreyi** (Upanishadic); Apala, Ghosha, Lopamudra, Vishvavara (Rigvedic hymn-composers).

q: What was the name of Janaka's brother?
explanation: In the Ramayana (Bala Kanda) Janaka's younger brother is Kushadhvaja, king of Sankashya, whose daughters married Bharata and Shatrughna. Nimi was the dynasty's founder.

notes.text: - Vedic people were skilled in **astronomy** (Vedanga Jyotisha), **mathematics** (Sulbasutra geometry) and **medicine** (Atharvaveda) – **not chemistry**.

q: Who is the Guru of King Janaka?
explanation: In the Ramayana Janaka's guru and family priest is Shatananda, son of sage Gautama (Shatananda Gautama); of the options only Gautama fits. Vishvamitra was a visitor, Vasishtha the Ikshvaku priest, Rishyashringa Dasharatha's ritual priest.

notes.text: - Vedic people were skilled in **astronomy** (Vedanga Jyotisha), **mathematics** (Sulbasutra geometry) and **medicine** (Atharvaveda) – **not chemistry**.

q: Who told the stories of Mahabharata to Janamejaya?
explanation: Vaisampayana, Vyasa's disciple, recited the Mahabharata to King Janamejaya at his snake sacrifice.

notes.text: - **Atharvaveda**: earliest charms and spells; **Ayurveda ("Science of Life") first appears** here (its prime origin; PMF lists Ayurveda as Upaveda of the Rigveda); term **kshetra-patni ("mistress of the field")** originates here (UPSC 2026); Sabha and Samiti = "twin daughters of **Prajapati**"; mentions Pashupati; recensions **Paippalada, Shaunaka**; reflects non-Aryan beliefs.

q: Mahabharat is also known by the name
explanation: The Mahabharata's original name was Jaya (Jaya Samhita); it is also called Satasahasri Samhita.

notes.text: - **Samaveda** is **compiled from the Rigveda**: about 1,549 verses (1,875 with repeats), all but about **75** from the Rigveda (mostly Mandalas VIII and IX).

q: The Total Number of Puranas is
explanation: There are 18 Mahapuranas.

q: Complete narration of 'Dasavataras' was given in
explanation: The complete narration of the ten avatars is given in the Bhagavata (Maha-bhagavatam); the Mahabharata and Ramayana tell only some of them.

q: Karna exercised his divine weapon, given by Indra, to attack one of the following
explanation: In the Mahabharata Karna had to spend Indra's infallible spear (Vasavi Shakti), kept for Arjuna, on Bhima's son Ghatotkacha on the fourteenth night of the war. (Ghatotkacha here is the epic hero, not the Gupta king.)

notes.text: - **Trayi / Vedatrayi** = **Rig, Yajur, Sama**; Atharvaveda excluded (recognised later).

q: In which of the following subjects were the Vedic Aryans not proficient?
explanation:
APPSC key: Astronomy. The texts show Vedanga Jyotisha (astronomy), Sulbasutra mathematics and Ayurveda; chemistry is the only discipline absent (NextGen p.25).
The Vedic people were proficient in astronomy (Vedanga Jyotisha), mathematics (Sulbasutra geometry) and medicine (Atharvaveda, Ayurveda); chemistry was not a Vedic discipline. (official key: Astronomy)

notes.text: ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.21-24; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.143, p.149, p.152; old app notes 1:21

q: Taittiriya Upanishad belongs to which Veda?
explanation: The Taittiriya Upanishad belongs to the Krishna (Black) Yajurveda; Ayurveda and Dhanurveda are Upavedas, not Vedas.

q: Which of the following was not commented upon by Shankaracharya?
explanation: Shankaracharya wrote bhashyas on the Prasthanatrayi: the Upanishads, Brahma Sutras and Bhagavad Gita; he did not comment on the Rigveda Samhita.

notes.text: TABLE head: Mandala | Content

q: In the parlance of Vedic Literature this sentence is said to be prominent one.
explanation: 'Tat tvam asi' (That thou art), a mahavakya of the Chandogya Upanishad, is the celebrated Vedic sentence. The others are later devotional lines.

q: Where does the term "Gothra" occur for the first time?
explanation: The word gotra first occurs in the Rigveda, where it means a cow-pen or herd of cows; its lineage sense appears in the Atharvaveda and Later Vedic texts.

notes.text: - **Aitareya Brahmana**: origin of kingship, ten forms of government, Shudra as servant, first mention of the **Andhras** (Sunahshepa story).

q: Recently, the manuscripts of which one of the following has been included in the UNESCO's Memory of World Register?
explanation: In 2007 UNESCO inscribed 30 Rigveda manuscripts of the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune, in the Memory of the World Register.

notes.text: > Gopatha = Atharva; Jaiminiya = Sama; Purushamedha = Shatapatha.

q: What was the name of the Conch of Nakula?
explanation: In the Bhagavad Gita (1.16) Nakula blew the conch Sughosha and Sahadeva Manipushpaka; Panchajanya was Krishna's. (Mahabharata topic, moved.)

q: Who narrated the war of Mahabharat to Dhrita Rashtra?
explanation: Sanjaya, given divine sight by Vyasa, narrated the Kurukshetra war to the blind king Dhritarashtra (Bhagavad Gita is his report).

notes.text: TABLE head: Saying / story | Upanishad

q: Who is known as Radheya in Mahabharatha?
explanation: Karna is called Radheya after his foster mother Radha. Krishna, Arjuna and Dhrishtadyumna have other epithets.

q: For how many days Karna was the commander of Kaurava Military during Kurukshetra war?
explanation: In the Mahabharata Karna led the Kaurava army for two days (the 16th and 17th) after Drona, until Arjuna killed him.

q: Which Mahabharata warrior was also known as Gudakesh?
explanation: Gudakesha ('conqueror of sleep') is an epithet of Arjuna in the Mahabharata/Bhagavad Gita.

q: Who killed Shakuni in Mahabharat war?
explanation: Sahadeva, the youngest Pandava, killed Shakuni on the 18th day of the Kurukshetra war.

q: Who wrote down the epic Mahabharatha while Vyasa was dictating?
explanation: By tradition Ganesha wrote down the Mahabharata as Vyasa dictated it. Shiva, Narada and Vishwakarma are not the scribe.

notes.text: - **Prasthanatrayi** = **Upanishads, Brahma Sutra** (Badarayana), **Bhagavad Gita**; the **Bhagavata is not** included. **Shankaracharya** wrote bhashyas on these three – **not on the Rigveda**.

q: Who is the father of Bhishma?
explanation: Bhishma (Devavrata) was the son of King Shantanu and the river Ganga.

q: Who has recited the 'Vishnusahasranama' for the first time?
explanation: In the Anushasana Parva of the Mahabharata, Bhishma recites the Vishnu Sahasranama to Yudhishthira.

notes.text: > Satyameva Jayate = Mundaka (not Mandukya); Jabala Upanishad is a different, later text.

q: Which Vedic text first refers to money lending?
explanation: The Shatapatha Brahmana has the first reference to money-lending; it calls the usurer kusidin.

notes.text: - Mimamsa is a darshana, **not** a Vedanga.

q: Who was the father of Dhruva?
explanation: In the Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas Dhruva is the son of King Uttanapada and Suniti. Karna, Dasharatha and Nahusha are unrelated.

notes.text: # Ramayana

q: One of the sons to Atri, one among the Sapta Rushies (Seven Rushies) and his wife Anasuya.
explanation: Durvasa was a son of Atri and Anasuya (with Dattatreya and Chandra). Vishwamitra, Ashtavakra and Jamadagni were not.

notes.text: - **Vaisampayana** told it to **Janamejaya**; **Ugrashrava Sauti** narrated it to Shaunaka's sages at **Naimisharanya**.

q: Who narrated Bhagavata Puranam to Parikshita Maharaja?
explanation: Sage Shuka (son of Vyasa) narrated the Bhagavata Purana to King Parikshit; Suta later retold it to Shaunaka and the sages. (Off-topic; moved.)

notes.text: # Mahabharata

q: Who is Vaikhanasa?
explanation: Vaikhanasa was a sage (maharshi) to whom the Vaikhanasa Agama of temple worship is traced.

notes.text: - War at Kurukshetra for **18 days**; Arjuna's grandfather = **Vichitravirya** (Pandu's nominal father); Karna spent Indra's **Vasavi Shakti** on **Ghatotkacha**.

q: Eka Vimshathi in Bhagavatham represents this
explanation: 'Ekavimsati' (twenty-one) in the Bhagavatam refers to the 21 avataras of Vishnu listed in its first skandha.

notes.text: - By **Vyasa**; original **Jaya / Jayasamhita** (8,800 shlokas) → Bharata → **Shatasahasri Samhita** (~1 lakh verses), **18 books (parvas)**, **Harivamsa** appended; older than the Ramayana; Bhagavad Gita (part of it) in **Sanskrit**.

q: The name of the mountain which was used to churn Ksheera Sagara
explanation: In the Samudra Manthan legend the gods and asuras used Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the serpent Vasuki as the rope to churn the Kshira Sagara. Off-topic (mythology), moved.

notes.text: - By **Valmiki**: **24,000** verses, 7 kandas, five stages from the 5th century BCE; Rama first met Hanuman in the **Kishkindha Kanda**.

q: Who is the Guru (Teacher) of demons (Rakshasulu)?
explanation: Shukracharya (Shukra, son of Bhrigu) is the guru of the asuras/rakshasas; Brihaspati is the guru of the devas, and Vibhishana and Mairavana are Ramayana characters. (Off-topic; moved.)

notes.text: - **Janaka**'s brother = **Kushadhvaja** (king of Sankashya); Janaka's family priest-guru = **Shatananda**, son of sage **Gautama** (the Upanishadic Janaka learnt from Yajnavalkya).

q: What is the name of Vasishta's Cow?
explanation:
Most books and keys: Nandini (Mahabharata). The Valmiki Ramayana calls the same cow Shabala (Sabala).
Vasishtha's wish-fulfilling cow, coveted by Vishvamitra, is called Nandini (daughter of Kamadhenu) in most books and keys. Off-topic (epics), moved.

notes.text: - **Samudra manthan:** serpent **Vasuki** was the churning rope.

q: Astadhyayi was written by
explanation: Panini wrote the Ashtadhyayi, the Vedanga text on Sanskrit grammar.

exam: APPSC Zilla Sainik Welfare Officer (Sainik Welfare Service)
q: Ashtadhyayi, the Sanskrit Grammar book was composed by
explanation: Panini composed the Ashtadhyayi, the Sanskrit grammar.

q: Who wake up Sri Rama by singing Kausalya Supraja Rama...?
explanation: In the Bala Kanda of the Ramayana, Vishwamitra wakes Rama with 'Kausalya supraja Rama' on the way to his yajna. Vasishtha was the family preceptor.

q: Who was the mother of Shatrughna?
explanation: In the Ramayana, Shatrughna (twin of Lakshmana) was the son of King Dasharatha and Queen Sumitra; Kaikeyi was Bharata's mother.

q: Who has instigated Ravana to abduct Sita?
explanation: In the Ramayana, Ravana's sister Surpanakha, insulted by Lakshmana, urged Ravana to abduct Sita. Mandodari was Ravana's wife and Tataka a demoness killed by Rama.

q: Name the son of Ravan who was killed in the hands of Lord "Hanuma".
explanation: In the Sundara Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana, Hanuman kills Ravana's young son Aksha Kumara at the Ashoka grove. Indrajit (Meghanada) was killed by Lakshmana; Mahodara and Mahaparshva were Ravana's commanders, not sons killed by Hanuman.

q: Sabari was in the Ashram of
explanation: In the Ramayana, Sabari served in the ashram of sage Matanga near Pampa and waited there for Rama. (Moved to ancient literature.)

q: What is the real name of Indrajit?
explanation: Indrajit, Ravana's son, was born Meghanada; he got the name Indrajit after defeating Indra. Akshakumara was another son of Ravana.

q: The other name of Vedic text is
explanation: The Vedic texts are Shruti ('heard'), revealed to the rishis; Smriti, Bhashya and Sutra are later classes of texts.

q: Which saint turned the Sagara Kumaras to ashes?
explanation: In the Ramayana and Puranas, the 60,000 sons of King Sagara, searching for the sacrificial horse, disturbed sage Kapila, whose glance burnt them to ashes; Bhagiratha later brought down the Ganga to redeem them.

notes.text: - **Kapila and the sons of Sagara:** in the Ramayana and Puranas the sage **Kapila** burnt the 60,000 sons of King Sagara to ashes; Bhagiratha brought the Ganga down to redeem them.

q: Jaimini commented on 'Purva Mimamsa'. Who commented on 'Uttara Mimamsa'?
explanation: Uttara Mimamsa (Vedanta) is ascribed to Badarayana, author of the Brahma Sutra, who is identified with Vyasa. Patanjali founded Yoga, Gautama Nyaya and Kapila Samkhya (an old APPSC key giving Kapila is wrong).

notes.text: - **Uttara Mimamsa = Badarayana = Vyasa** (APPSC G1 2002) – not Kapila, Patanjali or Gautama; an old APPSC key giving Kapila is wrong.

q: Which of the following does not constitute a part of the Shad-Darshanas (six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy)?
explanation: The six darshanas are Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa and Vedanta; Smriti is a class of texts (remembered tradition), not a school.

notes.text: - **Not among the six:** **Smriti** (a class of texts), **Lokayata** (Charvaka materialism), **Kapalika** (a Shaiva sect) (UPSC 2014), Charvaka, Ajivika.

q: Jaimini was the exponent of Purva Mimamsa. Who was the exponent of Uttara Mimamsa?
explanation: Uttara Mimamsa (Vedanta) is ascribed to Badarayana, author of the Brahma Sutra, who is identified with Vyasa. Patanjali founded Yoga, Gautama Nyaya and Kapila Samkhya (an old APPSC key giving Kapila is wrong).

notes.text: - **Uttara Mimamsa = Badarayana = Vyasa** (APPSC G1 2002) – not Kapila, Patanjali or Gautama; an old APPSC key giving Kapila is wrong.

q: Who is the wife of God Indra?
explanation: Shachi (Indrani), daughter of the asura Puloman, is the wife of Indra. Rati is Kama's wife; Menaka and Urvashi are apsaras.

q:
Select the correct statements about religious beliefs of the Rig Vedic Period :

I. Dyus was a celestial God of the Rig Vedic Aryans similar to Jupiter of the Greeks.

II. Prithvi was considered as the mother of all Gods.

III. Agni was worshipped as the intermediary of taking the offerings to the deities.

IV. Cow sacrifice was also the part of worship.
explanation: I, III and IV: Dyaus (Dyaus pitar) parallels Greek Zeus/Roman Jupiter, Agni carried offerings to the gods, and animal (including cattle) sacrifice was part of worship. II is wrong: Aditi, not Prithvi, was the mother of the gods.

q: The school of philosophy taught by Sankaracharya is
explanation: Shankaracharya (8th c., Kaladi) taught Advaita Vedanta – Atman and Brahman are one, the world is Maya. Vishishtadvaita is Ramanuja's, Dvaita Madhva's, Dvaitadvaita Nimbarka's.

q: Which philosophical theory was propagated by Kumarila Bhattu?
explanation: Kumarila Bhatta was the great exponent of Purva Mimamsa (ritual Mimamsa), defending Vedic ritual against Buddhism. Uttara Mimamsa is Badarayana's, Advaita Shankara's and Dvaita Madhva's.

notes.text: - **Shankara:** founded **four mathas** – **Sringeri** (south), **Puri** (east), **Dwarka** (west), **Badrinath / Jyotirmath (Joshimath)** (north); not Prayag, Kanchi or Varanasi. Called a "**crypto-Buddhist**" (Buddhist in disguise). Also Dashanami order and Panchayatana worship.

q: Which of the following spiritual doctrines was propagated by Kumarila Bhatta?
explanation: Kumarila Bhatta was the great exponent of Purva Mimamsa; Yogachara is a Buddhist school, Uttara Mimamsa is Vedanta and Jnana Marga the path of knowledge.

notes.text: - **Shankara:** founded **four mathas** – **Sringeri** (south), **Puri** (east), **Dwarka** (west), **Badrinath / Jyotirmath (Joshimath)** (north); not Prayag, Kanchi or Varanasi. Called a "**crypto-Buddhist**" (Buddhist in disguise). Also Dashanami order and Panchayatana worship.

q: Which philosophical theory was propagated by Kumarila Bhatta?
explanation: Kumarila Bhatta was the great exponent of Purva Mimamsa (ritual Mimamsa), defending Vedic ritual against Buddhism. Uttara Mimamsa is Badarayana's, Advaita Shankara's and Dvaita Madhva's.

notes.text: - **Shankara:** founded **four mathas** – **Sringeri** (south), **Puri** (east), **Dwarka** (west), **Badrinath / Jyotirmath (Joshimath)** (north); not Prayag, Kanchi or Varanasi. Called a "**crypto-Buddhist**" (Buddhist in disguise). Also Dashanami order and Panchayatana worship.
